title: Dressing up for Southern audiences and her view of race
summary: She kept evening dresses on the bus to look nice for audiences, which people said other singers did not. Dance asks about dances split by race; Humes says she never thought about color, since her father dealt with white realtors on equal terms.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, it was something else. I'll tell you. And I used to have alot of the kids when I'd go down to the South. And you know I always kept my evening dresses on the bus where I could change my clothes. And the different people would come and they would say, ' you know Miss Humes, you're the only singer that comes down here that dresses up for us'. I said, "really?" They said, "usually whatever they have on on the bus, that's what they come out and sing in".
I said, "oh, I don't understand that because we're working for you just like anybody else".
So they'd say, "well you're the only one that always trys to look nice for us".
"I'm working for you so I want to look as nice for you as I would for anybody else".
Some of those dates in the South there, would have a dance that would be for the white people and then afterwards you'd play for the colored

people and so on. And they weren't always a comfortable situations, were they?

No. To me, I don't know nobody no color. You know, my father, he was in real estate and he worked with white realtors, you know, and sometimes he'd have to go and visit with them. We'd go to their house and we'd not go to no back doors.
It was just like everybody else. I don't know that much about it myself.
